title: AFRINTEL Annual Cyber Threat Intelligence Report - Africa 2024
compatibility_note: The total_victims field is retained for historical compatibility; it refers here to incidents published and tracked by AFRINTEL, not to compromises that are all confirmed.

1. executive_summary.content: AFRINTEL documented 118 incidents across 27 African countries: 86 ransomware claims, 29 data leaks, and 3 access sales. No defacement is present in the dataset. South Africa accounts for 30 incidents, followed by Egypt with 13, then Algeria and Nigeria with 7 each. These figures measure observed publications, not the exhaustive incidence of cyberattacks across the continent.
key_findings: Ransomware: 86 incidents, or 74.1% of the dataset
South Africa: 30 incidents, including 29 ransomware publications
Second half: 70 incidents, compared with 47 in the first half
Monthly peaks: August and November, 15 incidents each
Finance / Banking: leading sector with 15 incidents

2. methodology.content: The twelve monthly victims.md files are the English source. They are synchronised with victims_FR.md in French. Ransomware, data leak, access sale, and defacement remain separate categories. A claim, a repost, a sample, and an official confirmation do not carry the same evidential weight.
limitations: Visibility bias arising from the public, criminal, and OSINT sources monitored.
Unclaimed or unpublished incidents may escape collection.
The frequent absence of public DFIR reporting limits attack-chain analysis.
Publication dates do not necessarily date initial access or exfiltration.
Reposts and duplicate claims can distort the perceived timing of activity.

4. incident_type_analysis.ransomware: Ransomware accounts for nearly three quarters of the dataset and is especially concentrated in Southern Africa. A victim listing on a leak site does not by itself establish encryption, exfiltration, or service disruption.
4. incident_type_analysis.data_leaks_and_access_sales: The 28 leaks and 3 access sales are more geographically distributed. Advertised access signals possible exposure but confirms neither current validity nor use.

5. sectoral_impact.content: Finance leads with 15 incidents, followed by government with 12. Manufacturing, professional services, and technology each account for 11. Priorities include identity and transaction protection in finance, public-service continuity, industrial segmentation, and control of supplier access.

observed.finding: 86 of 118 incidents are classified as ransomware.
South Africa accounts for 25.9% of the annual dataset.
The second half has 70 incidents, compared with 48 in the first half.

assumptions.confidence: Medium at the general level, low per incident
assumptions.finding: Credential reuse, initial access brokers, and exposed Edge or VPN services are priority research scenarios, not facts attributed to the victims in the dataset.

intelligence_gaps: Very limited availability of public African DFIR reports.
Initial access vectors, dwell time, and exfiltration paths unknown in most cases.
Age and completeness of several datasets undetermined.
Effect of reposts and duplicate claims on the timeline.

8. objective_comparative_analysis.assessment: The second half contains 23 more incidents, entirely driven by ransomware. Leaks decline slightly. This comparison describes the collected corpus and does not prove an equivalent increase in real compromises; source activity, reposts, and collection delays remain visibility factors.

10. recommendations: Require phishing-resistant MFA for sensitive and remote access.
Segment IT, industrial, administration, and backup environments.
Monitor bulk exports and govern third-party access.
Test continuity of essential services and offline recovery.
Regularly assess Internet exposure and close unnecessary remote access.

11. soc_recommendations.observed: Correlate organisations, domains, dates, and actors in the dataset with IAM, EDR, VPN, WAF, DNS, proxy, and mail telemetry.
11. soc_recommendations.assumption: Hunt for access from unusual infrastructure, credential reuse, account creation, privilege escalation, and bulk exports.
11. soc_recommendations.preventive: Detect LSASS dumping, obfuscated PowerShell, backup deletion, mass encryption, and abnormal outbound transfers, including through Rclone.

12. strategic_recommendations.observed: Prioritise ransomware resilience in Southern Africa and data-exposure risk in North and West Africa.
12. strategic_recommendations.assumption: Audit access scenarios involving identities, suppliers, and edge devices without presenting them as historical facts.
12. strategic_recommendations.preventive: Reduce the external surface, patch Edge/VPN appliances, close unnecessary RDP exposure, and maintain immutable, isolated, tested backups.

sections.13. conclusion: The 2024 dataset provides a working base to turn dark-web, darknet, and OSINT signals into defensive priorities. Its main limitation is the shortage of public DFIR reporting: observed facts, assumptions, and unknowns must remain explicitly separated.
